title: Cheryl Lerena
eyebrow: Writer · the poems, the books, the jar
dek: Her collection «Poems, Writings & Diary of a «Nutter»», transcribed entire and in her own order — 111 pieces of verse with every word of prose she set around them.
living: **Cheryl Lerena is living.** This archive's rule for the living is **name only** — no dates, no places of residence, no photographs — and that rule is kept here. What is published is **her work**, at her son's request, and nothing about her life.
lead:
She is a **writer**, and the folder says so before a word is read: **eight book projects**, one redrafted **eleven times between 2005 and 2020**; a shelf of short stories; a writers' group, *The Write Company*, with its exercises and its poetry competition.

Most of the poems below come from a page **she assembled and titled herself** — *«Cheryl Anne Lerena Defranceski — Poems, Writings & Diary of a "Nutter"»* — where she introduces her own work in her own voice: *«this is another heartbreaking poem I wrote to him»*, *«so I wrote a poem»*. **This is her selection, not the archive's.**

The largest thing in it is a **pandemic diary in verse** — at least a dozen dated poems from March 2020 into 2021, ending in a death. It is the most sustained piece of writing she has left, and nobody had ever set it out in order.

poems.title: Infidelity
poems.occasion: Her own note: after «*a long standing affair, committing adultery for years without me even suspecting, until I received a phone call from "the other woman"*», her marriage to **her first husband** was over. «*I wrote this poem after he pleaded with me to stay. It speaks for itself.*» — **She entered it in The Write Company competition and came 2nd.**
poems.conf: doc — signed, dated by circumstance, and placed in a competition
text: Do you want me to bleed?
poems.note:
**It is not written in her own voice.** It is a **dramatic monologue spoken by the man** — the refrain *«Please don't go / I love you so»* six times over, and underneath it every excuse in order: *just one more chance, you're to blame, I didn't mean to, it was the heat, it won't happen again, I was weak.* The rhymes are nursery rhymes. The last stanza is a threat.

A judge placed it **second**. She gives the man the microphone and lets him convict himself in couplets.

poems.title: So much hurt and pain
poems.occasion: Her note: «*This was the confusion and uncertainty about my life. Ivan and I always struggled to be together. I'm uncertain of the dates the following poems were written but it was some time in 1993.*»
poems.conf: doc — dated by her to about 1993
text: we'll find a way to be together
poems.note: Thirteen lines of pure interior argument, and then the fourteenth breaks format entirely — one word, in capitals, standing alone: **FOREVER**. It is the only shouted word in her poetry.

poems.title: Forever
poems.occasion: Her note: «*After moving from Durban to Johannesburg, Ivan and I still had interference and were tormented still trying to be together where we belonged. This is another heartbreaking poem I wrote to him in this tumultuous time.*» Signed **«From 'Muffet' to I.D. with love»**.
poems.conf: doc — introduced and signed by her
text: To you I give not myself
But my son, the one and only
I will be lost and lonely
I will shed many a tear
Keep him safe, happy and secure
You will be in my heart
My heart belongs to you forever
Say I do not love you
Sweet happy memories I will cherish
Of all the wonderful happy moments
I will hold dear in my heart forever
poems.note: **«To you I give not myself / But my son»** is one of the hardest first lines she wrote, and she never explains it. The pet names at the foot — *Muffet*, *I.D.* — are the only signature.

poems.title: Insanity
poems.occasion: Filed under **My Books** as a work in its own right. An earlier copy carries her own heading: «*Sitting at Café Bon-Bon in Bedfordview*» — so the poem has a **place of composition**, which nothing else here does.
poems.note: Written **at a table in a coffee shop**. *«Memories that flood / Like the drawing of Blood»* is the image it is built on — memory as something drawn out of you by a needle, against your will. She capitalised *Blood* and left it that way.

poems.title: Dark and lonely
poems.occasion: Her single line of introduction: «*This is my translation of how I felt when the end was nearing.*»
text: Drawing in an ocean of tears
Vision clouds as thoughts flow through poisoned veins
As the misery of yesterday slips into a tunnel of oblivion
Light seeps as the nothingness arrives
poems.note:
No rhyme, no metre, and the longest lines she ever wrote. It moves one way only — *screams* to *numbness* to *nothingness* — and the verbs turn passive as it goes, until the last thing that acts is not her. **«Death lusts»** is two words and it is the middle of the poem.

It is the only poem here with a **reader** in mind: she calls it a *translation*, as though the feeling were a language somebody else would need help with.

poems.title: A heart breaks
poems.occasion: Undated. It follows the Paputchka elegy in her own arrangement.
poems.note: Seventeen lines, none longer than four words, running a single night into a day and back to sunset. The only thing that develops is the pain: it *eats*, then it **feasts**. The heart is never *hers* — never *my* heart, always ***a*** heart.

poems.title: A poem for our grandchild
poems.occasion: Dated **13 August 2016** and headed «*A POEM FOR OUR GRANDCHILD **(Alessio)** – by Cheryl Anne Defranceski*». **Alessio was born the following March.**
text: We have not met you..... yet
to see if you're a boy or girl
to count your fingers and your toes
and feel the softness of your nose
to touch your skin and hear your cries
and smell the sweetness of your flesh
to gaze deep in your eyes
and whisper softly in your ears
our endless love for you always
And as we wait with bated breath
for you who we have not yet met
sleep well sweet child until it's time
for you to safely leave the womb
We wait for you with bated breath...
poems.note: Fifteen lines that never once say *I*. It is **«we»** all the way through, and almost every line is a **sense**. A poem about a person who does not exist yet, written entirely out of what it will be like to have a body near you.

poems.title: lub-dub
poems.occasion: Dated **5 February 2019** and headed «*POEM BY Cheryl Defranceski for our unborn grandchild **(Mateo)***». **The companion to the Alessio poem, written two and a half years later for the second boy.**
text: as you flourish in the womb
safe in the womb all the while
poems.note: **Two grandsons, two poems, and both written before the child existed.** Where Alessio's poem is built on the five senses, Mateo's is built on **one sound**, repeated six times — the heartbeat on a scan. It opens and closes on it, so the poem has no last word, only a last beat.

poems.title: Deda Baba
poems.occasion: Dated **23 May 2020**, and elsewhere introduced by her: «*My grandson Alessio calls me Baba or Babi and Ivan Deda. He thinks of the two of us as one. So I wrote a poem.*»
text: In the eyes of a child we are one
In the eyes of a child we are one
In the eyes of a child we are one
poems.note: The two names run together into one word — **DedaBabaDedaBaba** — and it beats. **The *lubdub* is carried over from Mateo's poem**, written fifteen months earlier: the same heartbeat, now belonging to a marriage instead of a foetus. The marriage vow — *till death us do part* — is dropped in the middle without ceremony.

poems.title: Ode to a beggar
poems.occasion: From the **Writers Write course, 2004**. The exercise was: *a stinking suppurating tramp collapses in front of you*. Her prose answer ends *«He is just a stranger. You have your own problems. You run away as fast as you can.»* Then she wrote the poem **from his side**.
text: How 'bout it lady, gimme a dime
Thank you lady I'm outa the sleaze
poems.note: She wrote the tidy middle-class answer the exercise wanted, and then **turned round and wrote the beggar**. The rhyme is deliberately crude and the last six lines abandon sentences altogether for a string of verbs — *snatch, grab, yank, pull* — so the mugging happens **in the grammar**. It is the most technically ambitious thing in the folder and it came out of a classroom drill.

poems.title: Tired, oh so tired
poems.note: It ends on a sound rather than a word — **«Quiet..... sssshhhhh»** — which is the only time she lets a poem stop by going quiet instead of by finishing.

poems.title: Sad, oh so sad
poems.note: ***«Like a thief / Slithering into crevices»*** is the line she reuses, word for word, in the **2021 elegy for her sister** — written for a private grief eighteen months before she gave it to a virus.

poems.title: An indestructible love
poems.occasion: Undated. The only poem here written in long lines.
text: Pillows separate where heads once rested together
When once they clasped tightly together
Bodies that held each other tight
Eyes that met and held a gaze forever
Words spoken with compassion and care
How did this indestructible love become so fragile and destructible
poems.note: Built entirely on **pairs coming apart** — two pillows, two hands, two bodies, two pairs of eyes — and it ends by turning its own title inside out: *indestructible* becomes **destructible** in the last four words.

poems.title: Like a pendulum
poems.note: The pendulum is the form as well as the subject — *to and fro* twice, *tears fall* at both ends. And the **sharp dagger** returns from the poem of 1 June 2020, so the two are a pair.

poems.title: I had a darling sister
poems.occasion: Written for the **first anniversary** of her sister's death and read to the family. **Catherine Tersia Lerena, «Rene», 21 May 1952 – 30 September 1999.** It stands inside a memorial address, set as ordinary paragraphs — which is why nobody had ever seen it as a poem.
poems.conf: doc — signed at the foot of the document it stands in
text: A dream her life was not
She knew pain as her friend
poems.note: Nine lines, no rhyme, ending on an ellipsis rather than a full stop. **«She knew pain as her friend»** is the line it turns on. It is not a comfort and does not try to be.

poems.title: If love could change the way things are
poems.occasion: A few paragraphs below «I had a darling sister», in the same memorial address.
text: If love could change the way things are
You would live forever and go so far
You'd know that I am always there
That I'll always love you, I'll always care
poems.note: It sits immediately before the sentence *«In October of 1992 a card arrived in the mail … here it is, I will share it with you»*. So it may be hers, or the verse off that card. **Printed as uncertain rather than claimed or dropped.**

poems.title: Two sides
poems.occasion: Dated **12 July 2017**. From her Word files rather than the compilation.
text: That life has not one but two sides
Then the dark cold of night
That life has not one but two sides
Hear the laughter loud and clear
That life has not one but two sides
Taste the words of kindness and love
Spit out the words of lies and hate
That life has not one but two sides
Smell the sweetness of a rose
and the stench of a titan arum
That life has not one but two sides
To the tale of two sides
To the tale of two sides
poems.note: The most **built** thing she wrote, and it comes straight out of the 2004 course: one of the exercises was **«describe these abstract words through the senses»**, and she filled in *love, hate, jealousy, pity, lust, anger, greed* five senses at a time. Thirteen years later she used the drill to make a poem. The **titan arum** — the corpse flower — is somebody who went looking. The close swaps *eyes* for **ears**.

excluded.heading: Two poems that are not hers, and are not printed
excluded.text:
**«Life is a sojourn here on earth»** sits in a letter she wrote to her surviving sister in **November 1999**, six weeks after Rene died. It is by **Helen Steiner Rice**, the American writer of devotional verse whose poems went out on greeting cards by the million — almost certainly how it reached a Johannesburg letterbox. **In copyright. Not printed.**

**«Each day I love you more, today more than yesterday and less than tomorrow»** is a single line kept in the Poems folder. It is a translation of **Rosemonde Gérard**, *L'éternelle chanson*, 1889 — *«chaque jour je t'aime davantage, aujourd'hui plus qu'hier et bien moins que demain»* — one of the most quoted lines in French. **Not hers either.**

Both are named rather than dropped in silence, because **a woman keeping a poem she loves is not the author of it**, and an archive that prints everything in a folder ends up attributing greeting cards to grieving people.

rest.heading: What else is in the folder, and why none of it is here
rest.text:
The poems are the smallest part of it. Also in the folder: **eight book projects** — *My Love Story*, redrafted eleven times from 2005 to 2020; *Husky*; *Soul Mates*; *A Murder*; *Desperate End*, whose first chapter was written for a creative-writing course and carries her name on the title; *Infidelity*; *Insanity*. Around **fifteen short stories**. Personal essays. A **writers' group** file thick with exercises, character sketches and competition entries.

**None of it is published**, and none of it is quoted here.

And a warning that has to be given plainly. **Several files in the Poems folder are not poems.** They are private prose, and some of it is about named living people — including her son — written in distress and never meant for a website. This archive has read them only far enough to know they are not verse, and has **published nothing from them, quoted nothing from them, and will not.**

If more of the writing is to appear, **it is Cheryl's to release, piece by piece.** This page will take whatever she gives it.

source: From the family's own writing folder, read 10 September 2026 at David's request. Poems transcribed exactly: line breaks, spelling, and the trailing ellipses are hers and are not corrected. «I had a darling sister» and «If love could change the way things are» come from the memorial address for Catherine Tersia Lerena, first anniversary, September 2000. Attributions for the two excluded poems: Helen Steiner Rice, and Rosemonde Gérard's «L'éternelle chanson», 1889. «My Gratitude Jar for the Year 2021» supplied in full by David, 10 September 2026, and quoted selectively.

pending.heading: A note on how this text was recovered
pending.text:
Her own compilation exists as a **screen capture**, not a document — three tall images with no text layer. The poems above were recovered by **optical character recognition** and then read back against the Word originals wherever both survive.

That means **small errors are possible**: a *«blowth»* that might be *«blow»*, an *«a physis»* that is almost certainly something else. Line breaks follow the capture. Where a reading looked wrong it was checked against the original file; where no original exists, the OCR stands and **may need her correction**.

Two poems — *«Gratefulness for 1 year»* and part of the Corona sequence — remain in **Apple Pages** format, whose text is compressed inside a binary this archive cannot decode. They need an export.

corona.heading: Reading the Corona diary
corona.intro:
**Twenty-three dated poems across twenty months**, in order. She gave the sequence an acrostic, and the acrostic is the argument:

> **C**apturing · **O**ur · **R**evelation **o**f · **N**ecessary · **A**cts

It is dated like a diary and rhymed like a nursery rhyme, and the pairing is the whole effect: *cobra* against *corona*, *sleaze* against *sneeze*, ***blowth*** — a word she appears to have made — against *growth*. **The lightness is not levity.** It is somebody rhyming her way through two years, and the rhymes hold until the last poem, when they stop mattering.

It is the largest single thing she made, and **nobody had ever set it out in order.**
corona.close:
Read the dates now that they are all here. **March is almost daily** — the 25th, 26th, 27th, 28th, 29th, 31st. **April is where she works hardest**: nine poems in twenty-six days, the 2nd, 4th, 10th, 13th, 17th, 19th, 22nd, 23rd, 25th and 26th. May brings the turn — *«Around the corner / Liberty peeks»*. Then July, three poems, and it stops.

**Fifteen months of silence.** The sequence resumes on **27 October 2021** by rewriting the hopeful poem of May 2020: the same fifteen lines, **one word changed at the end** — *«Lifting moods»* becomes *«Mood lifts»*.

**Eleven days later she wrote the elegy.**

elegy.heading: Reading the elegy
elegy.intro:
The sequence ends in one death. A sister she calls **«the older one, the wiser one»** and **«the Matriarch of our tribe»**, taken *«early hours Sunday morning»* — **Jeanette Riekstins, born Lerena, called Nita, who died on Sunday 6 June 2021.**

She wrote her sister's **whole life first**, in rhymed couplets, from a girl on a bicycle to a family of thirteen — and only then let the disease into the poem.

**Every one of the elegy's opening images is recycled from her own earlier poems.** *«Hidden from view / Like a sneaky shrew»* is the children's hygiene rhyme that opens the sequence. *«Slithering into crevices»* is the undated grief poem *«Sad, oh so sad»*. *«Like a bandit you came»* is 25 April 2020. She reached back through twenty months of her own writing and **built the elegy out of lines she already had**.

Then the rhyme abandons her. **«Scared and alone / Fighting for breath»** is the only place in a hundred pieces where she says what the dying was actually like, and it is six words long. What is left at the end is not verse — *«I hate you parasite / Perish you murderer / Suffocate and die»* — **a woman swearing at a virus**.

And before all of it she wrote her sister's **whole life**, in cheerful rhymed couplets, from a girl on a bicycle to a family of thirteen. **Forty-one lines, and thirty-three of them are a life being lived.** The disease gets eight.

dark.heading: Reading «Dark and lonely»
dark.text:
Among the poems she chose to publish is one she prefaces with a single line: ***«This is my translation of how I felt when the end was nearing.»***

It is printed here because **she printed it**, and because a collection of somebody's poems that quietly drops the darkest one is not their collection any more.
dark.note:
No rhyme, no metre, and the longest lines she ever wrote. It moves in one direction only — from *screams* to *numbness* to *nothingness* — and the verbs turn passive as it goes, until the last thing that acts is not her. **«Death lusts»** is two words and it is the middle of the poem.

It is the only poem here with a **reader** in mind: she calls it a *translation*, as though the feeling were a language somebody else would need help with.

jar.heading: My Gratitude Jar for the Year 2021
jar.intro:
A **third form**, and the one that turns out to hold the key to the elegies. Three hundred and sixty-five numbered slots, one line each, kept through 2021. She heads it with a list rather than a sentence:

> *Gratitude is attitude. Believe, receive, forgive, respect, heal, connect, feel, soul, truth, love, peace, purpose, harmony*

Most of it is small on purpose — that is the form. *«Rainy days.» «Waking each morning.» «Clean house.» «Good coffees.»* Her husband recurs as a running joke with three names: **«my indispensable Sous Chef»**, **«my in-house hairdresser — my man — PRICELESS!!!»**, and simply **«my Man who works hard in the garden»**. On two days in March she gives up on sentences altogether and writes one word: **«MEMORIES.»** **«FRIENDSHIPS.»**

shape.heading: The shape of it says more than the entries
shape.text:
She filled **180 of 365 days — forty-nine per cent** — and the pattern of the blanks is the year.

**January is complete.** Thirty-one days out of thirty-one, the resolve of a new jar. Then it thins to thirteen or fourteen a month and stays there.

**Except June.** June jumps back to nineteen — the fullest month since January — and June is the month her sister died. **She wrote more in the worst month of the year**, and what she wrote in it was gratitude.

And then: **December is empty.** Not thin — empty. The jar's last entry is **25 November**, and it is *«Chats with Dainis reminiscing about our beloved Nita.»* She never picks it up again. **The year does not end; it stops.**

june.heading: June
june.text: The entries around her sister's death are the reason this document matters to the archive as well as to the reading of it.
rows: **«That Nita did not suffer — her death came quick.»**
**«Alessio for his wise words "Babi I'll send an angel to heaven to bring your sister back".»**
«All the family and friends who attended Nita's memorial service (even with Covid)»
«To the Lerena family for attending Nita's memorial service, and Robert's kind words»
«Chats with Dainis reminiscing about our beloved Nita»  — *the last entry in the jar*
june.close:
**6 June 2021 was a Sunday.** The Corona elegy opens *«Then without warning / Early hours Sunday morning»* — and the sequence, the jar and the calendar agree. The sister of *«the older one, the wiser one»*, *«the Matriarch of our tribe»*, is **Jeanette Riekstins, born Lerena, called Nita**, and she died on Sunday **6 June 2021**.

That is a fact this archive did not have an hour ago, and it came out of **a gratitude journal**.

jar.quiet: What is not printed here is most of it. The jar names **living people** — a daughter-in-law, grandchildren, cousins, friends, an aunt, a hairdresser, a roofer — and it records **their surgeries, their test results and their falls** alongside the weather. Those entries are hers and theirs. **The form is published; the file is not.**

books.heading: The books
books.intro:
Eight projects sit under **My Books**, and two of them are the poems above — *Insanity* and *Infidelity* — filed as works in their own right. The other six are prose, and they fall into three groups.

**None of them is published here.** What follows is a **catalogue**: what each is, how long, and how long it took.

rows.sub: a memoir by «Mrs D» — filed as *My Love Story*
rows.d:
**Her life's work, and it is finished.** It began in **May 2005** at 1,908 words and reached its present length by 2016; there are **eleven drafts** in the folder, three of them named *Final*, *Final maybe 2* and *Final Maybe*.

It opens with a dedication to **her husband and her son**, and with an epigraph from **Oscar Wilde** — *«Death must be so beautiful … to have no yesterday, and no tomorrow. To forget time, to forgive life, to be at peace.»*

**Its subject is a lie she told and later confessed**, and it belongs to more people than her. **This archive describes it and does not quote it.** Whether any of it is ever published is not its decision, or David's alone.

A story in which a woman called **Anne** cannot prove that her sister **Kate** was murdered by Kate's husband, whose death was recorded as *«suicide — a murder of self»*.

**It is her own sister's death, written as fiction**, with the names changed and the facts kept. She wrote a **statement** of the same events in 1999; twenty years later she wrote it again as a novel, and the novel is the version in which somebody is guilty.

**Neither is published here** — the statement because it names a living man and makes criminal allegations this archive cannot test, the fiction because it is transparently the same man.

rows.sub: fiction — chapter one written for a creative-writing course
rows.d:
The same events again, and this time **from inside**. It opens *«Oh my God where am I? I can't breathe. Why can't I move?»* and it is the voice of a woman coming round in the dark, working out what has been done to her.

The file that carries her name in its title — *Cheryl Defranceski – Desperate End Chapter 1 Creative Writing* — is the coursework version. **She took the worst thing that happened to her family and made it an exercise in point of view.**

Opens: *«It's the year 2005. I'm forty-nine years old and looking forward to celebrating my fiftieth birthday this October. I'm alive. I'm happy to be alive.»*

Then, in the fourth paragraph, it becomes an account of **losing her faith** — convent, mass on Thursdays, confession on Saturdays — and of deciding that *«life after death is memories you pass on to your children»*. Which is, read at this distance, **a description of what she then spent fifteen years writing**.

rows.sub: comic memoir · «The lighter side of life with my pet Siberian husky»
rows.w: 455 words, plus a 950 KB illustrated file
rows.d:
Subtitled ***Life's a bitch then you buy one***. Paputchka arrives *«like a whirlwind … the ugliest little puppy I'd ever seen»* and ends up *«a snob and a true northern suburbs bitch»* who **can spell** — *«Do you want to go for a w-a-l-k?»*

The funny book has a companion piece that is not funny at all: an account of finding her under a palm leaf in the garden, *«sleeping»*, and of the first time she saw her husband cry. **It is the only subject she wrote twice, once for laughs and once for grief**, and the two together are the best prose in the folder.

rows.sub: filed as books; they are poems
rows.d: Both are printed above. That she filed them here — under *books*, each in its own folder, beside an eighty-thousand-word memoir — is worth noticing. **She did not rank her work by length.**

books.close:
Around it sits the rest of the writing shed: **fifteen short stories**, personal essays, and a **writers' group** file thick with exercises — describing *anger*, *greed*, *hate* and *jealousy* through the five senses, which is the drill that produced **«Two sides»**.

**Nothing in this section is published, and none of it is quoted beyond a line.** It is here so that the poems above are read for what they are: **not the occasional verse of somebody who did not write, but the shortest things made by somebody who wrote for twenty years.**

bio.heading: Who she is, in the only terms this archive is allowed
bio.text:
**She is living, so this page holds no dates, no places and no photograph.** What it can hold is **the work**, and there is a great deal of it.

She writes in **three forms and has done for twenty years**. There are **eight book projects**, the largest of them **eighty-one thousand words** and finished, begun in May 2005 and still being redrafted in 2020 — eleven versions, three of them called *Final*. There are **fifteen short stories** and a folder of personal essays. There is a **writers' group**, *The Write Company*, whose exercises survive: describe *anger*, *greed*, *hate*, *jealousy* through the five senses — the drill that later produced her best poem. And there is a **book club** with spreadsheets.

She writes **fast and short when it matters**. The pandemic gets a rhyming diary kept across two years. A grandchild gets a poem before he is born and a nursery rhyme at three. A dead sister gets a life in couplets. A year of gratitude gets three hundred and sixty-five numbered slots, of which she fills half.

**Her subjects are four**, and she returns to them the way writers do: **a marriage**, **a lie and its consequences**, **the deaths of two sisters**, and **a dog**. She wrote the dog twice — once for laughs, once for grief — which is as good a description of her range as anything an archive could invent.

And she is her own editor of last resort. She kept the poems in a folder called **Poems** and filed two of them under **Books** instead, beside the eighty-thousand-word memoir. **She did not rank her work by length.**

tree.heading: Where she stands
tree.note: Living people are **named only** — no dates, no places. The dead carry what the archive can prove.

nodes.d: his father from Argentina, his mother from England
named only as that, at David's instruction
living — named only · the compiler of this archive
living — named only · «a poem for our grandchild», 2016

tree.close: Two sisters dead **twenty-two years apart**, and a poem for each. It is the single fact that shapes everything on this page.

intro.heading: How to read what follows
intro.text:
The poems come in **three clusters**, and they are not arranged by quality.

**First the ones she wrote as poems** — signed, dated, filed under *Poems* or *Books*. These are the made things: *Two sides*, with the five senses hidden inside a refrain; *Infidelity*, spoken in a voice that is not hers; *A poem for our grandchild*, which never once says *I*.

**Then the Corona diary** — a dated sequence across two years, written the way other people kept sourdough. It is the largest single thing she made and **nobody had ever set it out in order.**

**Then the jar** — three hundred and sixty-five slots, one line each, which turns out to hold the date that fixes an elegy.

And two poems in the folder are **not hers at all**, which matters as much as the ones that are.

art.note: The illustrations were made to a written brief, one per poem, as a single matching commission — muted, painterly, **no faces and no lettering**: the poems are the text, and the living-people rule forbids photographs of her in any case. Each picture holds only what its poem holds.

preface.heading: Her own preface
preface.text:
She opens the collection herself:

> *I do not profess to be a poet or writer, however I do love to put down in words what often I cannot express. Psychologists believe «unhappy» people, «sad» people, «miserable» people, «depressed» people, write better than when feeling the opposite of these emotions. I tend to agree. I have had some miserable times in my life but the happy joyous elated times far exceed these and for that I'm extremely grateful. I'm privileged to be in this time called life with my loved ones, my reason for living.*

And then chooses an epigraph — **T. S. Eliot**:

> *POETRY IS NOT A TURNING LOOSE OF EMOTION, BUT AN ESCAPE FROM EMOTION; IT IS NOT THE EXPRESSION OF PERSONALITY, BUT AN ESCAPE FROM PERSONALITY. BUT, OF COURSE, ONLY THOSE WHO HAVE PERSONALITY AND EMOTIONS KNOW WHAT IT MEANS TO WANT TO ESCAPE FROM THESE THINGS.*

**A woman who does not profess to be a poet does not open with Eliot on impersonality.** The disclaimer and the epigraph disagree, and the epigraph is right.

No rhyme, no metre, and the longest lines she ever wrote. It moves one way only — *screams* to *numbness* to *nothingness* — and the verbs turn passive as it goes, until the last thing that acts is not her. **«Death lusts»** is two words and it is the middle of the poem.

how.heading: What this is
how.text:
Below is **her whole collection, in her own order, word for word**: the prose she wrote to introduce each piece, then the piece, then the next — exactly as it stands in the document she assembled and titled herself.

**Nothing is summarised and nothing is rearranged.** Where the archive has something to say about a poem it is set **underneath** it, in a smaller hand, marked as the archive's — never in place of her words and never before them.

The text was recovered by **optical character recognition** from a screen capture with no text layer, then read back against her Word originals wherever both survive. **Small errors are possible.** Where a reading is unmistakable — *«van»* for **Ivan**, *«lve»* for **Ive**, *«Iam»* for **I am**, *«IIL kill me»* for **I'll kill me** — it is corrected, because leaving a scanner's slip on the page is not fidelity to her, it is fidelity to the scanner. Where a reading is genuinely uncertain it is **left as scanned and flagged** rather than guessed: *«Even though a physis»* and *«Like the roots of a madrona»* both stand as the machine read them and both need her eye.

**One name has been removed at David's instruction.** Her introduction to the first poem names the man she was married to; this archive's rule is that **living people are named only, and never accused**, and an allegation of adultery against a named living person is not the archive's to publish. The sentence now reads *«my marriage was over»*. **Nothing else in her text is altered anywhere on this page** — this is the single exception, and it is recorded here rather than made silently.

**A note on stanza breaks.** The capture has no text layer, and the scanner inserted blank lines at its own tile boundaries rather than at hers. Rendering those as stanza breaks would **invent a shape she did not write**, so they are stripped and the verse runs continuous. Where the original stanza breaks are known — **from her own Word files, or from the page itself** — they are restored and the poem is marked **verified**. Five poems survive as Word documents and their structure is taken straight from them; the rest will be corrected as we work through them.

Where she gave a poem a **title** on its own line — *«Sitting at Cafe Bon-Bon in Bedfordview :-»* — that line is now read as a title rather than swallowed into the poem above it.

**One paragraph on this page is not from the scan.** The account of Paputchka's death was destroyed by the scanner — its opening sentence came back as *«WS CAPES FUG PS PEPE AU SII Pony FRU»* — and a filter of mine then deleted the whole paragraph with it. It is **restored word for word from the original document**, supplied by David, and marked here so that nobody has to wonder which text they are reading.
